newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM says Peru rebels plugged into mass media.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM says Peru rebels plugged into mass media.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said on Monday that Marxist rebels holding hostages in Lima were obtaining information on the Peruvian government's plans to end the crisis through the mass media.

Hashimoto, who has taken personal control of Japan's dealings with Peruvian efforts to end the siege at the Japanese ambassador's residence by the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MTRA), said Tokyo's priority remained the safe release of more than 100 hostages still held in the building.

"The MRTA is getting information from the mass media. I don't want to give them even one piece of information," Hashimoto told a new conference after receiving a first hand report on the situation from foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda.
There have been complaints among some Japanese journalists that Tokyo has put an unnnecessarily tight lid on information about the siege.
"We are doing our best to help win the safe release of all (the hostages)," Hashimoto said.
Hashimoto declined to comment on what steps the Japanese government will take to help bring the hostage crisis to a peaceful conclusion.
He also did not give details of his claim that the rebels were plugged into reports by the hundreds of journalists who have flooded into the Peruvian capital to cover the crisis.

However local journalists speculated that live television coverage and possibly reports available to the rebels on the Internet might be helping them to monitor security forces' movements outside the compound.
Ikeda, who spent four days in Lima as Japan's on-the-spot adviser, returned to Tokyo on Monday evening.
He said Japan would do its "utmost to to achieve the goal of winning the return of all those held hostage in a peaceful manner and as early as possible.
"In a sense, the most difficult task is still to come," Ikeda told reporters.

Japanese officials said in the past day Hashimoto has received letters of encouragement from U.S. President Bill Clinton, French President Jacques Chirac and British Prime Minister John Major. They said the world leaders all applauded Japan's handling of the crisis.
